summaries.example: Imagine several storybooks. One book tells of a bicycle race, another tells of a race where the bicycle has wings, and another tells of a race that cannot happen because the rules contradict each other. Leibniz would call the first two possible worlds: complete ways things could be. The third is impossible. He thought God chose the possible world that was best, while other possible worlds remained as ideas in the divine mind.
summaries.summary: Leibniz studied different ways reality might be: what must happen, what could happen, and what happens but could have been different. He imagined possible worlds as complete, orderly ways things could be. The things in one world must fit together; they cannot have properties that clash. Leibniz believed that every individual has a complete concept, meaning a deep description that includes the person’s whole history and future. He also thought that God knows all possible worlds and chooses the best one to make real. This does not mean every event is necessary. An action may be certain because it belongs to the world God chose, while another world could have contained a different action. In this way, Leibniz tried to connect God’s knowledge, the structure of nature, and human freedom.
key_ideas: Leibniz thought each individual has a very complete nature or idea that includes everything true about that individual.
A possible world is a way things could fit together without contradictions.
He said the actual world is the one God chose because it is best overall.
Something can be certain to happen in this world without being necessary in every possible world.
Leibniz used these ideas to explain how people can act freely even when their actions are known by God.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz’s ideas give us a careful way to talk about “could,” “must,” and “cannot.” They also help explain why philosophers ask whether a person could have acted differently, whether objects have essential features, and whether the world might have been arranged another way. His possible-worlds ideas later became important to discussions of logic and metaphysics.

important_terms.definition: A way things could be, including a set of things and the rules of nature that fit together without contradiction.
A statement or event that must be true and cannot be false without a contradiction.
A statement or event that is true, but could have been different in another possible world.
A group of things that can belong together because they do not contradict one another.

questions_to_think_about: Could a story describe a world that is possible but never becomes real?
What is the difference between something that must happen and something that happens for a reason?
If a person made a different choice, would Leibniz say it was the same person or a different possible person?

summaries.example: Consider Caesar crossing the Rubicon. In Leibniz’s actual world, this event is certain given the world God chose and Caesar’s complete individual concept. Yet it is not absolutely necessary: a different possible world could contain a Caesar-counterpart who remains in Gaul, because that alternative does not involve a contradiction. Leibniz therefore distinguishes certainty within a world from necessity across all possible worlds. He does not, however, think the very same individual travels between worlds; a fully determinate individual is world-bound.
summaries.summary: Leibniz’s modal metaphysics investigates necessity, possibility, impossibility, and contingency. Its foundation is his theory of individual substance: every individual has a complete individual concept containing, or making derivable, all truths about that individual across time. A possible world is a collection of compossible individuals governed by a coherent order of laws. Other possible worlds are not parallel physical universes; they have reality as possibilities in the divine understanding. Leibniz’s account of modality is related to possible-worlds semantics: necessity is truth in every possible world, possibility is truth in at least one, and contingency involves truth in the actual world with a contrary true in another. Yet Leibniz explains these notions through infinite analysis. Necessary propositions eventually resolve into identities, whereas contingent truths have an endless series of reasons connected to God’s choice of a world. His complete-concept theory supports a strong form of essentialism and appears to deny strict transworld identity: a changed “Adam” or “Caesar” would be a counterpart, not the numerically same individual. These claims generate a problem for freedom. Leibniz answers that an action can be certain given the actual world without being necessary in itself, because its contrary remains possible. God chooses the best world, characterized by a balance of simple laws and rich phenomena, though Leibniz also describes possible essences as striving for existence. The entry presents debate about how these explanations fit together.
key_ideas: A world is not merely a collection of objects; it also includes a system of laws and purposes that makes those objects and their histories fit together.
Leibniz’s modal vocabulary can be translated into possible-worlds terms, but his own explanation also depends on the analysis of concepts and truths.
Necessary truths reduce, through analysis, to identity; contingent truths have reasons but their analysis never reaches a final identity for finite minds.
Leibniz’s account of individuals creates a debate between ordinary essential properties, such as being human, and individuating properties that make one person that particular person.
His theory of freedom is compatibilist: an act can be determined by an individual’s complete nature and still be free when it flows spontaneously from the person’s perception of the best option.
Leibniz explains actuality mainly through divine choice, while also discussing the metaphor that possible essences strive for existence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Leibniz’s framework connects metaphysics, logic, theology, and the philosophy of action. It clarifies several distinctions still used in philosophy: necessity versus contingency, possibility versus actuality, and identity versus similarity across possible situations. It also shows why a deterministic-looking theory need not simply identify freedom with randomness. At the same time, the tensions among complete concepts, divine choice, essentialism, and responsibility give philosophers difficult questions about whether freedom requires genuine alternatives and how reasons can determine without necessitating.

important_terms.definition: Leibniz’s idea that an individual has a complete concept from which all truths about that individual—past, present, and future—can in principle be derived.
A set of individuals whose properties, perceptions, and governing laws can coexist without contradiction.
A truth that holds in every possible world and whose denial would produce a contradiction.
A truth that holds in the actual world because of the world’s freely chosen order, although its contrary is possible.
The view that each individual has at least one essential property; Leibniz is also presented as tending toward the stronger view that every individuating property is essential.
The stronger claim that every property of an individual is essential to that individual, so changing any property would produce a different individual.
Leibniz’s account of truth in which necessary analysis reaches an identity, while contingent analysis continues through an unending chain of reasons.
The claim that God selects the world with the simplest laws and the richest, most valuable outcomes.

questions_to_think_about: Does a complete description of an individual make that individual’s actions necessary, or can the actions remain contingent?
Is a person in another possible world the same individual, or only a counterpart resembling the actual person?
How does the distinction between certainty and necessity affect judgments about responsibility?
Can the claim that this is the best possible world be tested, or does it depend on Leibniz’s account of God and perfection?
Is the theory of striving possibles a rival explanation of creation or a metaphor for divine evaluation?

summaries.example: Suppose a school play has two possible scripts. In Script A, Maya joins the debate team; in Script B, a similar Maya joins the art club. Each script includes many details about the school, the rules, the other students, and what happens next. The two scripts are possible if their details fit together. Leibniz would not say that the exact same Maya moves from one script to the other. Instead, each script contains a complete individual with a different full story. The actual script is the one God chose because Leibniz thought it was best overall.
summaries.summary: Leibniz’s modal metaphysics asks what could happen, what must happen, and what happens but could have happened differently. He begins with individuals. Each individual has a complete concept: an ideal, fully detailed account containing all of the individual’s past, present, and future truths. Individuals belong to worlds, but not every collection of individuals can make one world. They must be compossible, meaning that their properties, experiences, and histories do not contradict one another. A possible world also has its own laws of nature. Leibniz believed there are many possible worlds, although only one is actual. These worlds are not separate physical planets existing alongside ours. They are complete possibilities understood by God. His views resemble the later philosophical method of defining possibility as truth in at least one possible world and necessity as truth in every possible world. Still, Leibniz also explains necessity through analysis: necessary truths can ultimately be reduced to identity, while contingent truths have reasons extending through an endless chain. This helps him argue that an event can be certain given the world God created without being necessary in itself. Human actions arise from a person’s own nature and judgment, so Leibniz presents freedom as compatible with determination. His theory also leads to a strong debate about essentialism. If an individual’s complete concept changes, Leibniz seems to treat the result as a different individual, although less complete descriptions can identify counterparts across worlds.
key_ideas: Leibniz thought there are many possible worlds, not just the one we experience.
A possible world must contain compatible individuals and a consistent set of natural laws.
He distinguished necessary truths, such as truths reached by identity, from contingent truths about the world God selected.
A person’s complete concept includes all of that person’s actions, but those actions can still be contingent rather than logically unavoidable.
Leibniz’s view suggests that a different version of a person in another world is a counterpart, not literally the same person.
He argued that God chose the best world, while also discussing a picture in which possible things compete or strive to exist.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas help us examine everyday words such as “could,” “must,” and “might.” They also introduce major philosophical questions about identity, choice, prediction, and responsibility. Leibniz is important because he tries to hold together several commitments at once: an orderly world, divine knowledge and goodness, many unrealized possibilities, and meaningful human freedom.

important_terms.definition: A complete way the universe could be, including people, events, and laws that fit together without contradiction.
Things that can exist together because their features do not clash.
True in every possible world; its opposite would create a contradiction.
True in the actual world but able to be false in another possible world.
The complete idea of an individual, containing everything true about that individual over time.
The view that some features belong to a thing so deeply that it could not exist without them.
A reasoned process that continues without end when explaining a contingent truth.

questions_to_think_about: Can two different stories both describe ways the world could be, even when only one becomes real?
Why might Leibniz say that a different choice would belong to a different counterpart?
How can an action be certain in one world but not necessary in every world?
What might make one possible world better than another?
Does knowing what someone will do take away that person’s freedom?
